# 00. Core principles

This chapter is the short version of the book. It sets out forty principles for designing a roguelike, the twelve disagreements a designer most needs to settle for their own game, a brief to work through when starting a new design, and suggested routes through the eighteen chapters that follow. Everything here is developed at length elsewhere in the bible, and each principle points to where.

The bible is a synthesis of what practitioners said in 311 talks given at Roguelike Celebration between 2016 and 2026: developers of shipped games, toolmakers, researchers, artists and players. It is not a proof. A principle appears here because several of those people arrived at it independently, usually in different years and about different games, or because it is the idea a whole chapter rests on. Where the support comes from fewer voices, the text says so. The principles are written as imperatives because that is how a designer uses them, but each one is a summary of what speakers reported working, and every cited statement links to the moment in a talk where someone said it.

Use the chapter in three ways. Read the principles as a checklist against a design you already have, and argue with the ones that do not fit; they are meant to be specific enough to disagree with. Read the fault lines before you commit to a direction, because they mark the places where credible designers chose differently and the choice depends on your game. And use the design brief at the start of a project, when the questions are cheapest to answer.

## The principles

The principles run from the inside out: what a run is for, how death and chance shape it, how the player learns it, the systems they act through, the generators, the story, and the interface, tools and process.

### What a run is for

**1. Decide whether your game is about mastering a challenge or inhabiting a world, and make every system answer to that choice.**
Zeno Rogue names the two approaches, mastery of a challenge and immersion in a complex simulated world, and designs HyperRogue for mastery ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 19:02](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1142)); Max Kreminski values roguelikes for trying to be worlds that exist independently of the player ([Max Kreminski 2018, 3:13](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=193)). George Moromisato sets NetHack's mastery and variety against a AAA game's one-time experience and production quality ([George Moromisato 2016, 7:41](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=461)), and in Q&A suggested, without being certain, that these contrasts are sliders a designer balances rather than a binary ([George Moromisato 2016, 29:43](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1783)). Tarn Adams adds why the choice matters: even "replayability" means different things (mastering interactions, being surprised, inhabiting a world) depending on which flavour of roguelike you make ([Tarn Adams 2018, 3:35](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=215)). See [01. What is a roguelike?](01-what-is-a-roguelike.md).

**2. Treat permadeath, procedural generation, consumables and turns as one package: for every part you drop, decide what now does its job.**
bhauth describes the parts as leaning on each other: permadeath forces players to replay the start, which needs procedural generation for variety, whose uneven difficulty needs consumables, which need turns in which to use them ([bhauth 2020, 12:24](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=744)). Max Kreminski, following Kate Compton, defines a genre the same way, as mutually supportive patterns that shore up each other's weaknesses, so that adopting a few pulls a design toward the rest ([Max Kreminski 2018, 5:46](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=346); [Max Kreminski 2019, 25:04](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1504)). Several of these parts began as answers to technical limits rather than as doctrine: Aaron A. Reed notes that early games generated worlds because a hand-made one would not fit in memory ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 2:05](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=125)), and the Rise of the Roguelite panel's moderator traces permadeath and level randomness to constraints that later games feel obliged to justify in fiction ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 33:08](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1988)). So keep each part for what it does in your game now, not because the genre always had it; Eiríkr Åsheim, for one, values Rogue's use of procedural generation to minimise assets for the permacomputing values it serves today ([Eiríkr Åsheim 2024, 6:30](https://youtu.be/qogCwa12jEg?t=390)). See [01. What is a roguelike?](01-what-is-a-roguelike.md) and [02. History and lineage: where the conventions came from](02-history-and-lineage.md).

**3. When you take roguelike structure somewhere new, name the element you are borrowing and adapt it to its new home rather than copying the surface.**
Shawn Main reduces the roguelike to a framework other genres can use: mutually exclusive choices that grow the player's power, varied and escalating challenges that test them, and a run that ends ([Shawn Main 2021, 7:25](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=445); [Shawn Main 2021, 8:00](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=480)). The successful transplants in the talks each picked one element on purpose: Against the Storm distilled a city builder's first hours into a run ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 2:28](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=148)), and Legends of Runeterra used runs to restore the power progression its generous card collection had removed ([Shawn Main 2021, 3:54](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=234)). Gillian Smith describes a university that keeps runs but drops permanent failure so students take risks, and contrasts that with points-and-badges gamification, "chocolate-covered broccoli" ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:02:05](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3725); [Gillian Smith 2026, 1:03:38](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3818)). Tyriq Plummer shows two platformers borrowing nearly the same roguelike mechanics and feeling completely different, because which mechanics you borrow and how you apply them matters more than the proportion ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 14:57](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=897)). See [18. Beyond roguelikes](18-beyond-roguelikes.md).

### Death, difficulty and randomness

**4. Keep permadeath for what it does to decisions, and make sure your game has choices that matter only because they cannot be undone.**
On the Rogue panel, Glenn Wichman proposed calling permadeath "consequence persistence": if players could save, drink an unknown potion and restore, the whole mystery-item mechanic would disappear ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712)), and the panel added that good outcomes are as permanent as bad ones ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 29:34](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1774)). bhauth argues permadeath makes players weigh probabilities across a huge space of outcomes, and compares a roguelike without it to poker with save and reload ([bhauth 2020, 13:09](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=789)). Sersa Victory uses the same irreversibility against consumable hoarding, since a run cannot be retried ([Sersa Victory 2022, 28:40](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1720)). If nothing in your design depends on irreversibility, permadeath is only a penalty. See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md).

**5. Make every death legible: the player should be able to say what killed them and what they would do differently.**
George Moromisato credits NetHack's "stupid deaths" with sustaining play because the player always knows exactly why they died and believes they could have avoided it ([George Moromisato 2016, 11:08](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=668)). Andrew Aversa defines good roguelike difficulty as challenges that are understandable, with the player feeling responsible for their death ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 2:51](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=171)); Alan Malloy calls a fun death one that carries a tactical lesson, not one avoidable only by grinding ([Alan Malloy 2017, 32:06](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1926)); and Gillian Smith says failure is fun only when it is normalised, with players able to name what they carry away from it ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:06:50](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4010)). Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup's morgue files show how: they record the messages before death and a snapshot of the map, so players can reconstruct who dealt damage and from where ([Quinten Konyn 2025, 4:21](https://youtu.be/a9flzzXJVcg?t=261)). Jeff Lait shows the cost of failing at this: players who fail at a long-term loop often do not recognise it and simply call the game bad ([Jeff Lait 2025, 5:19](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=319)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md) and [04. Learning and discovery](04-learning-and-discovery.md).

**6. Get the player from death to the next real decision in seconds, and spend your variety on the opening that every run replays.**
John Harris puts it simply: the longer a roguelike takes to start playing, the worse it is ([John Harris 2021, 17:10](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1030)). Lisa Brown found Nuclear Throne, which gets you back into play in about five seconds, stickier than Enter the Gungeon with its longer death sequence ([Lisa Brown 2020, 9:28](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=568)). Because default permadeath promises that early content will be seen again and again, Andrew Aversa argues for investing heavily in early-game variety ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=786)), and Shawn Main for distinct enforced starting positions such as NetHack's classes or Hades' first-room boon ([Shawn Main 2021, 17:32](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1052)). The same arithmetic rules out long story at the start: Tim Keenan calls intro cutscenes and story that replays every run a burden ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:44](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=224)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md).

**7. Carry knowledge, options and story across runs before you carry raw power.**
Several talks put the player's knowledge at the heart of the genre: it is what survives permadeath, and learning across runs is the progression a roguelike really offers ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 3:13](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=193); [Jim Shepard 2017, 5:39](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=339); [Tariq et al. 2016, 17:58](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1078)), and Arvi Teikari describes Noita relying on that knowledge instead of unlocking more powerful items ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 28:41](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1721)). Shawn Main argues that players want their time rewarded ([Shawn Main 2021, 22:07](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1327)), but Jim Shepard shows what meta power costs: too much makes the early game a walkover, and tuning late content for players who have died many times builds a grind wall for first-run players ([Jim Shepard 2017, 12:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=744)). The safer forms in the talks speed up the early game instead of raising the ceiling ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 9:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=558)), unlock options that widen future choices ([Jim Shepard 2017, 8:11](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=491)), let the world respond to past runs without changing difficulty ([Jim Shepard 2017, 13:38](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=818)), or, in Nic Junius's braided narratives, advance someone's story on almost every run ([Nic Junius 2024, 24:50](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1490)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md) and [12. Narrative and worldbuilding](12-narrative-and-worldbuilding.md).

**8. Let randomness set the problem rather than decide the outcome, and trim the extremes that a short run cannot average out.**
Shawn Main separates setup randomness, met before the decision and experienced as novelty to adapt to, from results randomness, where a roll decides the outcome and players feel they lost to the dice ([Shawn Main 2017, 4:58](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=298); [Shawn Main 2017, 5:51](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=351)). Subset Games describe Into the Breach as moving randomness to the input, with random spawns but deterministic player actions ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 18:09](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1089)), and David Dunham moved Thousand Hells from opaque dice to a visible shuffled deck ([David Dunham 2026, 7:06](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=426)). Evan Debenham explains why randomness still needs shaping: a single run is too short for outcomes to converge, so smooth the extremes while keeping the game exciting ([Evan Debenham 2022, 5:47](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=347); [Evan Debenham 2022, 1:39](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=99)); Sébastien Benard starts from a balanced, non-random allocation and adds chaos back on purpose ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:59](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1739)), and Brogue paces its reward rooms on a rubber band ([Brian Walker 2018, 14:00](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=840)). Main also marks the limit: smooth away all the variance and the game becomes flat micro-optimisation ([Shawn Main 2017, 19:57](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1197)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**9. Price every action, especially waiting.**
Nicholas Feinberg's test is to imagine a player with infinite patience and ask whether their win-maximising use of a system is fun ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 0:28](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=28)); if it is not, the design suffers even for players who never do it, because after each death they suspect they lost by skipping the grind ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 5:55](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=355)). Feinberg traces the problem to actions that cost nothing, above all nearly free out-of-combat turns ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 11:19](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=679); [Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 14:02](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=842)). The evidence comes from several directions: hunger exists to turn time into a resource weighed against other options ([Rosalind Miles Chapman 2020, 2:06](https://youtu.be/j9ykOdQRUQk?t=126); [Shawn Main 2021, 18:42](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1122)); Tangledeep became trivially easy when its hunger clock was removed while health still regenerated, because players could kite and wait ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 12:44](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=764)); and Angband's players turned out to win more games per hour by diving than by the cautious play the community long thought optimal ([Nick McConnell 2021, 7:13](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=433)). Dylan White adds the opposite failure: time is a resource in itself, and in Rift Wizard players left spells unused because they did not feel worth a turn ([Dylan White 2021, 13:08](https://youtu.be/kvgKKRLil_8?t=788)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md), [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md) and [06. Combat and tactics](06-combat-and-tactics.md).

**10. Offer difficulty as granular, clearly labelled options, and design the softer modes rather than just switching death off.**
Andrea Roberts argues that because difficulty is subjective, players need tools to tune it themselves ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 18:16](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1096)), and Philomena Schwab that different players find different parts hard, so separate settings serve more of them than one slider ([Philomena Schwab 2022, 7:34](https://youtu.be/wLLDPz8PnQg?t=454)). Dan DiIorio answered conflicting "too easy" and "too hard" feedback with twenty unlockable difficulties rather than a new baseline ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 2:29](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=149)), and Roundguard learned to label its easy mode clearly after streamers equipped its mercy relic without realising what it was ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 23:25](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1405)). Andrew Aversa treats permadeath itself as a spectrum ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 5:06](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=306)): about 30% of Tangledeep's players chose its non-permadeath mode ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 10:18](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=618)), but hazards acceptable without permadeath feel unfair with it, so both modes need design work ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 16:58](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1018)), and the default mode shapes how players perceive the whole game ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 6:04](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=364)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md).

### Learning and legibility

**11. Teach principles, not routes: write down what separates an expert from a novice, and make sure the game itself can teach it.**
bhauth proposes judging a game by the difference between what new and very good players do, because that difference is what the game teaches ([bhauth 2020, 6:51](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=411)). Brian Walker and Herbert Wolverson independently credit random levels with moving the skill from memorising routes to mastering systems ([Brian Walker 2018, 0:46](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=46); [Herbert Wolverson 2020, 2:29](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=149)), Andrea Roberts contrasts rehearsing a Mario level with Spelunky's need for principles and improvisation ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 7:45](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=465)), and Pandamander describes roguelikes pushing players "out of book" into situations where they must generalise ([Pandamander 2024, 14:16](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=856)). Gillian Smith asks designers to decide what players should learn ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:26:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5214)), warning from teaching that the lesson actually learned is rarely the intended one ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:17:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4652)). Teaching should not interfere with that learning: Roberts limits Roundguard's tutorial to foundations ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 4:08](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=248); [Andrea Roberts 2020, 8:36](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=516)), and Luck be a Landlord and Magic: The Gathering pace complexity through rarity ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=670); [Gavin Verhey 2024, 4:38](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=278)). See [04. Learning and discovery](04-learning-and-discovery.md).

**12. Make the structure behind your randomness perceptible, or players will learn patterns that are not there.**
Emilia Lazer-Walker found that when players cannot model how inputs shape a generator, its output is indistinguishable from randomness, and cut Computational Flaneur's many sensors down to simple GPS regions ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:51](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1011)). Isaac Karth recommends foregrounding causality, as NetHack does by tracking the source of every damage instance for the death message ([Isaac Karth 2019, 23:49](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1429)). The failure is well documented: Rogue's players believed some games were "scroll heavy" when no such system existed ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 9:55](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=595)), Evan Debenham finds that uniform random ranges lead players to see patterns that are not there ([Evan Debenham 2022, 3:14](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=194)), and Max Kreminski warns that early streaks of true randomness give players a false picture of a generator before they have learned its baseline ([Max Kreminski 2017, 9:58](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=598)). See [04. Learning and discovery](04-learning-and-discovery.md).

**13. Choose what to hide, make everything else deducible inside the game, and make guesses cheap to test.**
Thomas Biskup calls it lazy design to make players look mechanics up in FAQs, and admits ADOM is guilty of it ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=955)); Jim Shepard says players should never need to go online to work out how to progress ([Jim Shepard 2017, 32:34](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1954)), and, of NPCs the player must woo, that guesswork is not gameplay ([Jim Shepard 2019, 21:19](https://youtu.be/LKCRim02opc?t=1279)). Mystery still has a place when it is chosen: Alexei Pepers separates productive uncertainty from the unproductive kind ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 35:32](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2132)), asks for very clear communication everywhere else ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 17:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1057)), and warns that suspense turns to frustration when testing a hypothesis is unfun or costly ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 21:28](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1288)). Jongwoo Kim's The Shrouded Isle makes hidden information fair with consistent rules and a way to investigate afterwards ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423)), and Nic Tringali's The Banished Vault shows every resource location while leaving its cost uncertain ([Nic Tringali 2023, 17:51](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1071)). Spoilers follow anything fixed: John Harris notes randomness only delays them ([John Harris 2016, 22:09](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1329)), which is why Caves of Qud generates disease cures each game and records them in an in-game book ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 9:05](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=545)). See [04. Learning and discovery](04-learning-and-discovery.md).

**14. Make threats readable and the odds countable, so the player is planning rather than guessing.**
Dan Norder describes the proto-roguelike Chase getting all its tactics from robots that always take the shortest route, so players can predict them exactly ([Dan Norder 2024, 3:54](https://youtu.be/ohH6LBM2EiU?t=234)); Tyriq Plummer credits Spelunky's forethought to simple, consistent enemies and traps ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 13:50](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=830)); Into the Breach is a fully visible puzzle ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 2:41](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=161)); and Scrubbin' Trubble displays enemy threat zones ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 6:46](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=406)). Albert Ford wants field of view symmetric and consistent with targeting ([Albert Ford 2020, 1:05](https://youtu.be/y1zkrTcNJbc?t=65)), Dylan White keeps Rift Wizard's damage formula simple enough to count hits exactly ([Dylan White 2020, 13:11](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=791)), and Evan Debenham finds randomness frustrates less when players have levers over the odds, such as Shattered Pixel Dungeon's guaranteed hits from stealth ([Evan Debenham 2022, 9:54](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=594); [Evan Debenham 2022, 10:15](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=615)). Nauticrawl shows the failure: in its real-time beta players died without understanding why, until the game created turns from its simulation ([Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 7:40](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=460); [Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 9:55](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=595)). See [06. Combat and tactics](06-combat-and-tactics.md) and [08. Monsters, NPCs and AI](08-monsters-npcs-and-ai.md).

**15. Watch newcomers play, and do not let veterans alone tell you what is clear.**
Andrea Roberts finds that much roguelike difficulty is knowledge veterans carry without noticing ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 5:24](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=324)): Roundguard's newcomers did not grasp that enemies hit back on contact ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 7:07](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=427)), Darren Grey describes FTL punishing players who bring a standard RPG's heroism ([Darren Grey 2020, 14:31](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=871)), and Tabea Iseli found that a non-violent game wipes out much of players' learned game literacy ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 15:30](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=930)). Thomas Biskup saw ADOM's interface, praised for years by its community, condemned on Steam ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 7:24](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=444)), and says an hour of observed play tests with no explanation taught more than twenty years of ADOM ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 19:09](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1149)). Watch rather than ask, since Max Sahin finds people are bad at naming their experience ([Max Sahin 2025, 1:46](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=106)), and seek out players unlike you: Alexei Pepers says only visually impaired testers show what blind players need ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)), and Michael Langford simulates pre-literate children by swapping a font for unreadable glyphs ([Michael Langford 2021, 10:24](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=624)). See [04. Learning and discovery](04-learning-and-discovery.md), [13. Interface and accessibility](13-interface-and-accessibility.md) and [16. Production and process](16-production-and-process.md).

### Systems, tactics and builds

**16. Build depth from interacting systems that follow one set of rules for player, monster and world, and write those interactions between properties, not between pairs of things.**
Brian Walker describes a roguelike as a chain of exciting situations, each a cognitively interesting puzzle ([Brian Walker 2016, 2:41](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=161)), and Darren Grey and Dan Recht trace those always-new problems to items and systems that interact and force trade-offs ([Darren Grey 2020, 12:16](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=736); [Dan Recht 2017, 4:26](https://youtu.be/FnJxkId-1eE?t=266)); Alice Lai counts such combinations as content alongside areas and monsters ([Alice Lai 2021, 4:50](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=290)). Dwarf Fortress defines every creature, the player included, with the same kind of file and rules ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 19:15](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=1155)), Plummer calls Spelunky's shared rule set for players, NPCs and items what makes it a roguelike ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 12:53](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=773)), and Bob Nystrom has player input and monster AI both produce the same Action objects ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 20:15](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1215)). To keep this tractable, NetHack reduces things to shared attributes such as materials and codes interactions between attributes ([George Moromisato 2016, 19:21](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1161)), immersive sims have objects emit and respond to stimuli instead of hand-coding brittle pairwise cases ([Rich Wilson 2021, 6:47](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=407)), and Ultimate ADOM derives abilities from body parts, so a creature without hands cannot open doors with no special code ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 23:19](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1399)). See [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md) and [15. Architecture and tools](15-architecture-and-tools.md).

**17. For every simulated reaction, ask how the player will see it and what decision it creates.**
Brian Walker prefers rich terrain to monsters because it explains itself and supports satisfying plans ([Brian Walker 2016, 18:50](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1130)), and Darren Grey describes Brogue letting a weak character be powerful by luring monsters into lava or setting fields alight ([Darren Grey 2020, 26:04](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1564)). Arvi Teikari reports the limit from Noita: many physically plausible reactions are interesting in themselves but hard to turn into decisions, and unlimited destruction quickly became boring ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 18:53](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1133); [Arvi Teikari 2021, 16:35](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=995)). Rich Wilson expects the hard work to move onto designers as fine-grained simulation becomes feasible ([Rich Wilson 2021, 26:51](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1611)), and Tyriq Plummer limited cascading effects in a multiplayer game because everyone had to stop and parse what had happened ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 7:16](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=436)). See [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md).

**18. Give every turn a real choice from a small set of verbs, and let movement do most of the work.**
Sersa Victory describes a turn as one mutually exclusive choice ([Sersa Victory 2022, 12:22](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=742)), and Darius Kazemi points to Hoplite, which offers only three or four choices but no move without consequences ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 31:01](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1861)). Michael Brough calls Rogue's bump-to-attack an elegant foundation, and shows its shared input letting Nightmare Cooperative move a whole party with one key ([Michael Brough 2021, 2:48](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=168); [Michael Brough 2021, 7:36](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=456)). NetHack keeps movement as the core command and hides rarer verbs in menus ([George Moromisato 2016, 17:17](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1037)), Brogue puts stairs in alcoves so that stepping onto them uses them ([Brian Walker 2018, 18:28](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1108)), and slashie argues for triggering actions contextually by moving rather than through menus ([slashie 2026, 9:08:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32933)). Thomas Biskup aims to get Ultimate ADOM by with about seven keys, noting that about 90% of ADOM players die within roughly 3,000 turns and never need the power commands ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 12:59](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=779)). See [06. Combat and tactics](06-combat-and-tactics.md) and [13. Interface and accessibility](13-interface-and-accessibility.md).

**19. Give each monster and hazard one clear trick that targets something other than hit points, and tie it into the game's other systems.**
Brian Walker compares monsters and effects to chess pieces that project distinct zones of jeopardy ([Brian Walker 2016, 21:59](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1319)); John Harris lists Shiren's monsters, each a distinct problem, from archers to one that turns your items into rice balls ([John Harris 2024, 7:10](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=430)); and Eric Billingsley keeps a small roster with one ability each so there is variety players can learn ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 8:44](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=524)). Readable behaviour can be very cheap: David Craddock notes that Rogue's monsters had minimal AI, yet players ascribed behaviour to them and learned to exploit what little there was ([David Craddock 2016, 5:05](https://youtu.be/Gs9Nb5ZYRY0?t=305)), while Jeff Olson's lasting regret about Alphaman is monster AI with too little variation ([Jeff Olson 2023, 11:45](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=705)). Traps show what goes wrong otherwise: Reed Lockwood calls the hidden, instant, single-tile damage trap a hit-point tax and makes tying traps into other systems the most important rule ([Reed Lockwood 2022, 2:48](https://youtu.be/ymgmhtkRLyY?t=168); [Reed Lockwood 2022, 10:13](https://youtu.be/ymgmhtkRLyY?t=613)), Angband's traps degenerated once every character could detect them easily ([Nick McConnell 2021, 13:04](https://youtu.be/LaOcggk7U88?t=784)), and Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans make combinations of hazards the challenge ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 28:41](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1721)). See [06. Combat and tactics](06-combat-and-tactics.md) and [08. Monsters, NPCs and AI](08-monsters-npcs-and-ai.md).

**20. Store character power in what the player finds, so the run changes shape as it goes and avoiding a fight becomes a strategy.**
Michael Brough traces the genre's basic arc to a rogue who becomes, in effect, a wizard by collecting magic items ([Michael Brough 2025, 44:25](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2665); [Michael Brough 2025, 32:21](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=1941)). Brian Walker replaced Brogue's skills with items and enchantment scrolls and removed experience points, so builds based on avoidance and trickery work ([Brian Walker 2016, 7:59](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=479); [Brian Walker 2016, 11:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=706)); Into Ruins does the same, and Eric Billingsley credits the change with more build variety and viable fleeing while conceding the loss of the feeling of growing stronger by killing ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 15:42](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=942)); and John Harris praises Brogue for it ([John Harris 2016, 5:22](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=322)). Item-based power is not the only answer: bhauth argues that Brogue's linear upgrade costs push players into one or two investments, while DCSS's skill costs support more viable builds ([bhauth 2020, 14:48](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=888)). See [07. Characters, items and builds](07-characters-items-and-builds.md).

**21. Let chance decide what is on offer and the player decide how deep to invest, and make each offer change how the run plays.**
Andrew Cedotal finds that neither fully constructed nor fully random upgrades sustain engagement, and recommends a "drafting mullet": chance limits the options, the player controls investment, as pick-one-of-three choices do ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 26:28](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1588); [Andrew Cedotal 2024, 27:08](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1628)). Lisa Brown describes players with low strategy motivation, Brown included, who want a small number of meaningful, reactive picks at regular points, such as Slay the Spire's post-combat card choice ([Lisa Brown 2020, 13:40](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=820)). Shawn Main asks that each choice be strong enough to change the style of the run and have no answer that is right regardless of the build ([Shawn Main 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=816); [Shawn Main 2021, 13:54](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=834)), and turning an option down should cost something, as in Brogue's treasure rooms ([Sersa Victory 2022, 13:07](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=787)) or Oath's either-or choices whose road not taken can haunt the player ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 22:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1341)). See [07. Characters, items and builds](07-characters-items-and-builds.md).

**22. Make synergies implicit and the build space well connected, and cap how much one run can absorb.**
Cedotal finds players credit more "comboness" to synergies that arise through other game systems than to ones printed on the upgrade ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:04](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=304)), and Ezra Szanton orders synergy sources from obvious callouts to obscure shared choices ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 18:53](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1133)). Shawn Main points to Dicey Dungeons, where choices act on shared building blocks so they interact readily ([Shawn Main 2021, 13:11](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=791)). Szanton warns that isolated synergy clusters make drafting shallow, because a committed player ignores everything outside the cluster, and wants a well-connected network with weak clusters ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 11:44](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=704); [Ezra Szanton 2025, 12:54](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=774)). At the other end, Alice Lai found that too many upgrades in one Hades run blend every build into "the same powerful sludge" ([Alice Lai 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=816)). See [07. Characters, items and builds](07-characters-items-and-builds.md).

**23. Let a rare, earned build break the game, but remove any option so strong that every run must take it.**
Dan DiIorio warns against balancing a single-player roguelike like a competitive game, because players have more fun becoming more powerful than their enemies ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 6:45](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=405)); Courtney Liessen notes that a broken combo lasts only until the run ends ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 11:46](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=706)) and that players delight in "cheating" the system as designed ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 2:54](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=174)); and the Against the Storm team deliberately sought the rare game-breaking build ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 5:32](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=332)). Brian Walker keeps effects strong and balances them by situation rather than by shrinking numbers ([Brian Walker 2016, 13:39](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=819)). The line falls at dominance: Pandamander warns against strategies that win every time ([Pandamander 2024, 15:21](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=921)), Against the Storm cut city walls because they would have been built every run ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 10:02](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=602)), and Andrew Aversa links Tangledeep's contradictory negative reviews to jobs far stronger or weaker than the rest ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 21:32](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1292)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md) and [07. Characters, items and builds](07-characters-items-and-builds.md).

### Generating worlds and content

**24. Decide what each generator should do to the player before you pick a technique, and budget for it as design work, not free content.**
Isaac Karth asks designers to say why they want to generate something and what effect it should have ([Isaac Karth 2019, 0:08](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=8)), Gillian Smith to choose generative systems like materials, by the experience you want ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:14:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4472)), and Alexei Pepers not to use procedural generation for every problem just because it exists ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 3:36](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=216)). The talks agree it does not save work: Brian Walker calls procedural level design a different skill, not an easier one ([Brian Walker 2018, 2:15](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=135)); Bruno Dias says generation is not a force multiplier for cheap content ([Bruno Dias 2016, 11:49](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=709)); Younès Rabii measures a generator's real cost in the designer knowledge encoded in it ([Younès Rabii 2025, 17:05](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1025)); and the Wildermyth team warn that honing generated content to quality takes substantial time ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 30:06](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1806)). What goes wrong otherwise is concrete: Santiago Zapata's detective game failed for lack of authored content to feed its engine ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 14:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=854)), and Gabriel Koenig found Jettomero's procedural systems added almost nothing because they ran entirely behind the scenes ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:03:00](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=3780)). See [10. Content generation](10-content-generation.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**25. Make variation players can perceive: commit each level or region to one strong idea, correlate what you generate, and keep a plain baseline so the rare stands out.**
Many talks independently warn that a generator can produce endless outputs players cannot tell apart, Kate Compton's "10,000 bowls of oatmeal" ([Isaac Karth 2019, 8:29](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=509); [Max Kreminski 2018, 14:36](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=876); [Darius Kazemi 2017, 10:17](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=617); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 16:01](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=961)). Rich Wilson found that mixing many small random elements into every level made them indistinguishable, so Prey: Mooncrash gave each level one dominant hazard ([Rich Wilson 2021, 19:04](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1144)); Isaac Karth points to No Man's Sky's single-biome planets and to landmark levels ([Isaac Karth 2019, 7:19](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=439); [Isaac Karth 2019, 14:53](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=893)). Alex Byaly shows that generating attributes independently makes every region a sample of the same distribution, and points to Tales of Maj'Eyal's correlated item bundles ([Alex Byaly 2022, 4:24](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=264); [Alex Byaly 2022, 7:09](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=429)). And outliers need ordinary neighbours: Cat Manning wants a few spiky characters against an unremarkable cast ([Cat Manning 2020, 16:20](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=980)), Elliot Trinidad gives Blaseball plenty of plain names so the wild ones stand out ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 11:45](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=705)), and Mini and Max's rare "atoms" extend novelty long after the common ones are familiar ([Jon Perry 2025, 16:06](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=966)). See [09. Level generation](09-level-generation.md), [10. Content generation](10-content-generation.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**26. Author the structure and generate the detail: give the generator a plan, and hand-made pieces wherever judgement matters.**
Dead Cells abandoned generated platforms because gravity makes jumps hard to get right, and hand-authors its rooms at two to five minutes each ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 14:18](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=858); [Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 16:29](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=989)), assembling them on a simple tree of nodes for entrance, exits, shop and treasure ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 20:51](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1251)). Spelunky's rooms are mostly fixed tiles ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 18:05](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1085)), Sergio Garces picks from about a hundred quickly authored layouts ([Sergio Garces 2022, 17:39](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=1059)), and NetHack mixes generated levels with fixed branches and special levels ([Adeon 2017, 6:27](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=387)). Joris Dormans gives the generator a plan as a graph of locks, keys and relationships ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 16:24](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=984); [Ian Holmes 2017, 14:02](https://youtu.be/b2VkgcC1xRc?t=842)), but warns that levels planned entirely in advance become fragile machines that collapse when the player deviates ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 20:07](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1207)). Local methods need the same frame: wave function collapse output looks the same in every direction, so Caves of Qud wraps its ruins in a higher-level structure ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 47:40](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2860)), and Emily Halina shows such methods producing dungeons with missing doors or unreachable rooms ([Emily Halina 2024, 22:26](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1346)). See [09. Level generation](09-level-generation.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**27. A generated space matters only if it creates decisions: size it from your movement rules, and give it loops.**
John Harris argues that if a random dungeon's contents do not challenge the player, its layout is meaningless ([John Harris 2016, 11:20](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=680)). Brian Walker builds space from overlapping zones with different advantages ([Brian Walker 2016, 16:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1006)), Loren Schmidt likens reading terrain to reading a Go board ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 5:01](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=301)), and Sersa Victory tunes generators to layer several choices into one encounter ([Sersa Victory 2022, 21:35](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1295)). Space must fit the rules that move through it: Chogue widened Rogue's corridors so bishops could leave the first room ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 10:14](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=614)), Wildermyth's generated maps failed large monsters that could not fit through narrow paths ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 21:42](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1302)), and Scrubbin' Trubble uses small stages so cooperating players stay together ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 6:54](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=414)). Trees and perfect mazes force one route; Brogue adds doors where two sides of a wall are far apart by path distance ([Brian Walker 2018, 4:49](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=289)), and Larn's imperfect mazes give navigation choices ([John Harris 2021, 24:54](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1494)). See [09. Level generation](09-level-generation.md).

**28. Guarantee whatever blocks progress, then look at your generator's output in bulk and in context.**
Herbert Wolverson's rule is to guide your randomness and then check the result ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 24:35](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1475)), culling unreachable regions with a Dijkstra map ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 19:27](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1167)); Jack Schlesinger uses a flood fill against dead ends ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 14:35](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=875)), and Brian Walker tolerates an occasional inaccessible reward room but never an unreachable staircase ([Brian Walker 2018, 30:04](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1804)). Randomly placed key items can create circular dependencies that make a game unbeatable ([Stella Mazeika 2019, 6:17](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=377)), so Jon Perry gives almost every gate in Planet Zoldath more than one solution ([Jon Perry 2025, 34:06](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2046)). Beyond correctness, expressive range analysis (scoring many outputs on metrics chosen for your game and plotting them) shows what a generator actually makes ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 2:44](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=164); [Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 5:04](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=304)), and Oliver Withington uses the plot to choose outliers and cluster representatives to inspect by hand ([Oliver Withington 2024, 12:50](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=770)). Mike Cook adds that a generator is best understood by how its output collides with the game's other systems ([Mike Cook 2026, 23:01](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1381)), and Schlesinger and droqen use solvers to judge the difficulty of generated puzzles ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 29:02](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1742); [droqen 2026, 24:56](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=1496)). See [09. Level generation](09-level-generation.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**29. Keep a human between the generator and the player, and plan for the meanings players will find in what it makes.**
Ben Berman observes that influential generated content usually relied on human curation ([Ben Berman 2017, 35:16](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2116)), Martin Pichlmair finds delight in generators where a person performs an activity and selects the result ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 14:54](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=894)), and Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans produced terrible creatures when the same process ran without the player choosing ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 13:15](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=795)). Robin Sloan rules out piping a language model's raw output to players, and heavily filters the quests generated for Sloan's own project ([Robin Sloan 2019, 11:21](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=681)), and Janelle Shane would not expose a generator to open player input, preferring to generate and hand-pick in advance ([Janelle Shane 2022, 21:25](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1285)), and Everest Pipkin calls choosing the source text the most important decision in generative text ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 10:39](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=639)). Players will read meaning into the output whether or not you meant any: Blaseball's fans formed deep attachments to players that were only names and a few facts ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 4:28](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=268); [Joel Clark 2020, 30:32](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1832)), Younès Rabii's flower generator produced shapes resembling fascist imagery ([Younès Rabii 2020, 8:01](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=481)), and Darius Kazemi recommends layered filters and a public takedown policy ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 32:32](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1952)). See [10. Content generation](10-content-generation.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

### Story, tone and meaning

**30. Build for the stories your systems produce, and leave gaps for the player to fill.**
Emilia Lazer-Walker argues roguelikes are better than any other genre at emergent storytelling ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 3:58](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=238)), and Tarn Adams notes that players retell what they did with buckets in Skyrim, never the scripted dragon fights ([Tarn Adams 2018, 7:18](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=438)). Adams names the conditions: mechanics that interlock, stay internally consistent and can be investigated ([Tarn Adams 2018, 3:08](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=188)); Jim Shepard adds that Dungeonmans' tone gives players a trellis for their own stories ([Jim Shepard 2016, 3:16](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=196)). Rogue's creators planned rich monster lives and found that players imagined the rest from rooms, letters and stats ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 10:49](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=649)), Dustin Freeman presents bare events so as not to take the player's interpretation away ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 10:53](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=653)), and Paul Dean argues that players can get the gist of a story from fragments, as in archaeology or a jigsaw ([Paul Dean 2025, 17:23](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1043)). Abstraction helps but does not work alone: Evan Ovadia found ASCII needs a small trigger of detail to evoke imagination ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=364)). See [12. Narrative and worldbuilding](12-narrative-and-worldbuilding.md) and [14. Art and audio](14-art-and-audio.md).

**31. Choose what to simulate knowing that players read your numbers and systems as facts about the world, and make fiction and mechanics push the same way.**
Xalavier Nelson Jr. argues that a game's generation systems and base numbers say more about its world than its writing does, and that even deciding what counted as an organ would be read as objective truth ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 18:44](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1124); [Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=331)). Ivy Melinda relays how Caves of Qud's inherited roguelike systems created a "combat gravity well" that made the game more bloodthirsty than intended ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 5:41](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=341)); Emilia Lazer-Walker warns that if your main verb is kill, players will resolve emergent situations with violence ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 22:24](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1344)); and Jongwoo Kim found that standard simulation models assume material growth, which undermined a story about belief ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 4:47](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=287)). Tim Keenan attributes the dislike of curated story in roguelikes to story and mechanics pulling in different directions ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:23](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=203)); done well, fiction sells a rule, as when Against the Storm turned a bare timer into an impatient queen ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 26:53](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=1613)). See [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md) and [12. Narrative and worldbuilding](12-narrative-and-worldbuilding.md).

**32. Write authored story for repetition and death: keep what replays short, release story across runs, and acknowledge what happened to each character.**
Tim Keenan and Andrew Aversa both warn that story replayed every run becomes a burden ([Tim Keenan 2017, 3:44](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=224); [Andrew Aversa 2020, 13:46](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=826)). Nic Junius finds branching narratives become untenable to author, and uses braided linear storylines released by conditions, with a cap on new story per run like Hades' ([Nic Junius 2024, 8:01](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=481); [Nic Junius 2024, 11:15](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=675); [Nic Junius 2024, 18:21](https://youtu.be/sOZH6RPuNJ8?t=1101)); Voyageur and Sunshine Shuffle use storylets gated by conditions ([Bruno Dias 2016, 15:17](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=917); [Stav Hinenzon 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=226)). Death itself is material: Harry Solomons calls the restart a powerful narrative tool ([Harry Solomons 2024, 24:30](https://youtu.be/AwOuZTCeOrU?t=1470)), and Duskers keeps discovered logs across deaths ([Tim Keenan 2017, 4:33](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=273)). Wildermyth makes generated heroes feel authored by having generation lead into handwritten content and by acknowledging what happened to them by chance ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 3:11](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=191); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 18:50](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1130)). See [12. Narrative and worldbuilding](12-narrative-and-worldbuilding.md).

**33. Log what your simulation does, sift it for drama, and give the player instruments to find it.**
Max Kreminski presents James Ryan's model in which emergent narrative is what results after events are chronicled, sifted and narrativised, not the raw output ([Max Kreminski 2019, 13:29](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=809)), and Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster agree that fluent, connected events do not by themselves make a story ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 5:37](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=337)). Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi of SIBR say surprising stories stay impenetrable without detailed records and that filtering is what turns data into narrative ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:01](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=181); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:28](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=208)); Kreminski's story sifters search a chronicle for sequences to surface ([Max Kreminski 2020, 1:34](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=94)). Without instruments, players are lost in a deluge of insignificant events ([Max Kreminski 2019, 11:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=701)), so Jasmine Otto lets players aim their attention ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 2:45](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=165)), Jonathan Lessard publishes a live, hyperlinked chronicle ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 4:32](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=272)), and Crusader Kings III, as Cat Manning describes, sums up hidden personality as a two-word epithet ([Cat Manning 2020, 19:11](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1151)). See [12. Narrative and worldbuilding](12-narrative-and-worldbuilding.md) and [13. Interface and accessibility](13-interface-and-accessibility.md).

### Interface, craft and process

**34. Put the depth in the rules, not in operating them: plan the interface from the start, never make the player wait, and automate decisions that have one right answer.**
Subset Games estimate that half or more of their development time goes to UX, and found early Into the Breach playtests painful because of presentation, not design ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 7:18](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=438)); Angband's maintainers made it approachable without making it easier ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 11:28](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=688)). Thomas Biskup keeps depth in the game logic and out of the interface ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:34](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=934)), designing Ultimate ADOM's interface simple-first because reducing ADOM's complex one proved a constant struggle ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 27:09](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1629)), and Josh Ge makes every action in Cogmind reachable by mouse ([Josh Ge 2016, 20:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1214)). Jeremiah Reid's rule is that animation never blocks input ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 11:16](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=676)), and Josh Ge, Angband and Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup automate no-brainer decisions, one-key targeting and exploration ([Josh Ge 2016, 22:56](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1376); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 13:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=807); [bhauth 2020, 3:43](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=223)). See [13. Interface and accessibility](13-interface-and-accessibility.md).

**35. Treat representation as a budget and an audience choice, and make whatever you draw read at a glance and hold together as one style.**
Santiago Zapata, Evan Ovadia and Josh Ge all note that characters make content cheap: a new monster costs a glyph, a colour, a description and its data ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 15:24](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=924); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=485); [Josh Ge 2018, 17:05](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1025)). Graphics reach a larger audience but cost accordingly: Zapata and Thomas Biskup say mainstream players expect them ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 15:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=949); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 16:42](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1002)), Zapata calls static sprites in place of letters a half-measure ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 16:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=977)), and adding graphics to ADOM took three and a half to four of the revival's five years ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 31:49](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1909)). Whatever you draw should read like a symbol: Joel Ryan gives tiles a few strong forms ([Joel Ryan 2022, 24:02](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1442)), and Subset and Marlowe Dobbe derive a creature's look from what it does ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1576); [Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 7:34](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=454)). And keep one style: Sergio Garces and Ovadia both warn that mixing assets from sources with different styles produces art that clashes ([Sergio Garces 2022, 6:30](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=390); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 5:16](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=316)). See [14. Art and audio](14-art-and-audio.md).

**36. Write the rules once and author content as data, so that adding one more item takes minutes rather than days.**
Kate Compton's rule is to author many pieces as static data run through one well-tested interpreter ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:43](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=823)), and the talks show the same shape in Ultimate ADOM, Caves of Qud, Cataclysm, Hades and Backpack Hero ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:58](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=958); [Ray 2023, 2:39](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=159); [Jeremy Rose 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=545); [Alice Lai 2021, 15:39](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=939); [Jasper Cole 2023, 7:57](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=477)); Spry Fox's tags let a newly tagged item flow into every loot table and shop automatically ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 5:57](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=357)). Know the limits of your format: Monster Train's one-script-per-effect cards broke down on dependent, scaling effects, leaving behaviour implicit in code and forcing custom code for specific cards ([Brian Cronin 2021, 12:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=725)). The payoff is speed: Thomas Robertson notes that if adding fire is easy you will add ice too ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 8:11](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=491)), Danny Day built two new Desktop Dungeons classes in a week ([Danny Day 2018, 23:36](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1416)), and Thomas Biskup added a spell to Ultimate ADOM in about eight minutes once the feature beneath it existed ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 4:49](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=289)). Data files also let players mod the game ([George Moromisato 2022, 18:31](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1111); [Josh Ge 2016, 6:48](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=408)). See [15. Architecture and tools](15-architecture-and-tools.md) and [17. Community and business](17-community-and-business.md).

**37. Seal a deterministic, serialisable simulation off from its presentation, and do it before you need it.**
Brian Cronin separates data, state, logic and presentation, keeps all state including the random number generator in one serialisable structure, and lets presentation learn about the world only from emitted change records ([Brian Cronin 2024, 8:54](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=534); [Brian Cronin 2024, 13:31](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=811); [Brian Cronin 2024, 20:11](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1211)); saves, replays and networking then follow ([Brian Cronin 2024, 25:33](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1533)), and a preview is just the real code run on a copy ([Brian Cronin 2024, 27:04](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1624)). Generation belongs inside the same discipline: Andrew Clifton derives random values from a hash of the situation and the game seed ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 0:46](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=46); [Andrew Clifton 2020, 6:05](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=365)), and Alexander Birke keeps Sea of Rifts deterministic so players' bugs can be reproduced ([Alexander Birke 2024, 3:40](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=220)). The cost of waiting is reported repeatedly: Monster Train's lack of determinism forced many preview exceptions ([Brian Cronin 2021, 8:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=486)), Danny Day found replays too complicated to retrofit ([Danny Day 2018, 22:21](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1341)), and ADOM's interface runs through all its code, which made a mobile version practically impossible ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=564)). See [15. Architecture and tools](15-architecture-and-tools.md) and [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**38. Scope to finish: ship something small first, prototype the core cheaply, cut whatever does not serve it, and multiply your estimate by four, then by four again.**
Josh Ge, Santiago Zapata, Jeff Lait and slashie all argue for finishing small games, because finishing is how you learn the whole process and get feedback ([Josh Ge 2018, 4:16](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=256); [Santiago Zapata 2016, 4:14](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=254); [Jeff Lait 2025, 3:20](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=200); [slashie 2026, 9:05:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32728)). Ge starts from a core mechanic explainable in one sentence ([Josh Ge 2018, 5:50](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=350)), Subset from a feeling ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 15:17](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=917)), and Tyler Robertson and Brian Cronin prototype in spreadsheets and Tabletop Simulator first ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 2:00](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=120); [Brian Cronin 2025, 1:48](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=108)). Matt Ritchie and Eric Billingsley cut anything that does not add to the core, including genre staples ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 4:48](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=288); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 11:06](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=666)), and Against the Storm declined features, even fantastic ones, that did not make runs differ ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 7:51](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=471)). Tyler Coleman's rule is to multiply any estimate by four and then by four again ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 10:37](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=637)); turning Cogmind from a 7DRL, a game made for the Seven Day Roguelike competition ([Andrew Doull 2025, 3:25](https://youtu.be/NaqP13nkpfU?t=205)), into a commercial one was expected to take a year and took nearly 6,000 hours over three and a half years ([Josh Ge 2016, 14:20](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=860)). See [16. Production and process](16-production-and-process.md).

**39. Treat what players tell you as a description of a problem, not a specification of the fix, and make sure someone triages all of it.**
Brian Cronin credits consistent triage, someone reading every report, as the main tool behind Monster Train's success ([Brian Cronin 2021, 18:11](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1091)). Evan Debenham works out the desire behind a suggestion ([Evan Debenham 2021, 11:42](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=702)), Andrew Aversa listens to the problem players describe but not necessarily the solution ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:23](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1043)), Subset diagnoses whether a complaint is about design, presentation or a wish for a different game ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 9:37](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=577)), and Chris King insists feedback is not a democracy ([Chris King 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/1Np1DSdpoR0?t=609)). Before changing course, weigh the quiet players: Angband's maintainers and Dan DiIorio both warn that the satisfied majority is silent ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 25:51](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1551); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 3:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=190)). And tend the community on purpose, since, as Caelyn Sandel warns, one left to form by itself is run by its loudest, meanest voices ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 22:15](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1335)). See [16. Production and process](16-production-and-process.md) and [17. Community and business](17-community-and-business.md).

**40. Build the means of sharing a run into the game: logs, morgue files, seeds and data players can pass around.**
Tariq, the developer of Catacomb Kids, argues that procedural generation loses much of its point without a community to compare runs with ([Tariq et al. 2016, 2:03](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=123)), and Ivy Melinda finds the gaps between players' different experiences of Caves of Qud fertile ground for fan work ([Ivy Melinda 2020, 7:55](https://youtu.be/db6S2lgTWmI?t=475)). Signet and Maliksi ask for scrollback and replays that are easy to view and share, and for safe public data ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 15:40](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=940); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 21:26](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=1286)); Alan Malloy describes DCSS saving a morgue file for every online game, which makes help requests answerable ([Alan Malloy 2017, 9:35](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=575)); and Mike Cook asks designers to inspect output at the cropped scale players actually share ([Mike Cook 2026, 22:02](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1322)). Drew Streib reports that live watching on public servers shortened NetHack's learning curve from years to weeks for many players ([Drew Streib 2016, 11:44](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=704)). See [17. Community and business](17-community-and-business.md).

## Fault lines

These are the questions where credible practitioners in the talks chose differently, and where the right answer depends on your game. Each is developed in the chapter's "Tensions and open questions" section.

**Should death be permanent by default?** Andrew Aversa argues permadeath should be the default only if you can deliver its promise of a varied, fun early game without a heavy opening story ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 24:30](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1470)). Against that, David Brevik resisted Blizzard's request to make Diablo real-time and drop permadeath, because turn-based play and permadeath were where a roguelike's tension came from ([David Brevik 2023, 6:58](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=418)), Todd Furmanski values the precarious power narrative it creates ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 4:47](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=287)), and Glenn Wichman points out that irreversibility is what makes decisions real ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 28:32](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=1712)). It depends on where your best content is: at the start of every run, or at the end of a long one. See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md).

**Should runs make the character stronger?** Shawn Main argues players want their time rewarded ([Shawn Main 2021, 22:07](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=1327)), and Jim Shepard that meta power softens permadeath and frees players to experiment ([Jim Shepard 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=564)). Arvi Teikari's Noita relies on growing knowledge rather than unlocking more powerful items ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 28:41](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1721)); Tim Keenan notes that purists find meta-progression grindy, though others like runs that differ because of what they have earned ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:42:37](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31357)); Aversa that it frustrates when it feels like required dying ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 26:31](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=1591)); and John Harris considers the Wii Shiren, which kept levels after death, the weakest in its series ([John Harris 2024, 19:48](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=1188)). It depends on whether your systems produce enough novelty for knowledge alone to keep runs fresh. See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md).

**How much should randomness be smoothed?** Shawn Main warns that smoothing out variance makes a game flat ([Shawn Main 2017, 19:57](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1197)), and Dylan Gedig accepts reduced agency in Peglin for memorable moments ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 25:03](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1503)); Evan Debenham and Sébastien Benard smooth deliberately ([Evan Debenham 2022, 1:39](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=99); [Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 28:59](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1739)). The tie-breaker offered at John Harris's talk is whether players can build intuition for the randomness ([John Harris 2016, 29:20](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1760)). Two cautions cut across both camps: Ben Berman warns pity systems can be addictive for people with gambling problems ([Ben Berman 2017, 33:30](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2010)), and Tyler Coleman that hidden fixed cycles may verge on dark patterns ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 28:40](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1720)). See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md).

**How hard should the clock push?** Tyriq Plummer removed starvation from Catacomb Kids because it punished caution and made pacifist runs impossible ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 21:50](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1310)), and Thomas Biskup made Ultimate ADOM's hunger weaken but never kill ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:56](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1076)). Andrew Aversa's Tangledeep collapsed into kiting without a clock ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 12:44](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=764)), and Nicholas Feinberg keeps Crawl's clocks weak because strong ones would push optimal players to turn off auto-explore ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 21:16](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=1276)). It depends on whether something else in your game already makes waiting costly. See [03. Death, difficulty and progression](03-death-difficulty-and-progression.md) and [06. Combat and tactics](06-combat-and-tactics.md).

**How much should stay hidden, and what about the wiki?** Alexei Pepers, Arvi Teikari and Leonard Richardson make the case for deliberate mystery, rare interactions found over many runs, and even misdirection ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 35:32](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2132); [Arvi Teikari 2021, 26:16](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1576); [Leonard Richardson 2017, 12:10](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=730)); Thomas Biskup, Jim Shepard and Andrew Aversa want mechanics deducible or presented in the game ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=955); [Jim Shepard 2017, 32:34](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1954); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 3:43](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=223)). On spoilers, Brian Walker warns that lookups make play rote ([Brian Walker 2016, 3:18](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=198); [Brian Walker 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=280)), while Jeremy Rose, Drew Streib and Max Kreminski defend outside knowledge as an encyclopedia, as insufficient to win, or as not worth fighting ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 19:23](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1163); [Drew Streib 2016, 25:22](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1522); [Max Kreminski 2017, 19:31](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1171)). It depends on whether the mystery is the game's subject with everything else clear ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 17:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1057)), and on who is playing: low-discovery players want rules exposed up front ([Lisa Brown 2020, 24:23](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1463)). See [04. Learning and discovery](04-learning-and-discovery.md).

**Few pieces or many?** Eric Billingsley argues fewer elements force you to tune every interaction and make a more learnable game ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 29:07](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1747)), Michael Brough that type-specific effects matter only when there are few types ([Michael Brough 2021, 17:00](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1020)), and Cole Wehrle that too much content makes a game feel arbitrary ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 19:31](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1171)). George Moromisato traces NetHack's difficulty and endurance to its breadth ([George Moromisato 2016, 12:05](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=725); [George Moromisato 2016, 25:05](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1505)), and Casey Yano's team found unlimited relics playtested better than a three-slot cap ([Casey Yano 2022, 7:37](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=457)). It depends on whether you want players to learn a system whole or spend years mastering a space. See [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md) and [10. Content generation](10-content-generation.md).

**How deep should the simulation go?** Brian Walker values terrain that explains itself and supports plans ([Brian Walker 2016, 18:50](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1130)), and Todd Furmanski would spend the gap between turns simulating weather and material chemistry ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 33:09](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=1989)). Arvi Teikari found that only a small set of Noita's material reactions were immediately interesting as gameplay ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 18:53](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1133)), Rich Wilson expects finer simulation to move the hard work onto designers ([Rich Wilson 2021, 26:51](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1611)), and Cat Manning warns that characters whose moods change too fast become chaotic and frustrating ([Cat Manning 2020, 26:15](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1575)). It depends on how much of the machinery the player can observe and act on. See [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md) and [08. Monsters, NPCs and AI](08-monsters-npcs-and-ai.md).

**Keep the leak or plug it?** Jason Grinblat argues that rough edges show a possibility space too rich to file down, and Caves of Qud turned a crash-prone body-swap exploit into a feature ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 16:59](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1019); [Jason Grinblat 2021, 18:22](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1102)); Blaseball adds new systems on top of broken ones ([Joel Clark 2020, 13:31](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=811)). Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup excludes powerful but tedious mechanics on principle ([Alan Malloy 2017, 30:55](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1855)), and Liza Knipscher allows no clever workarounds in a simulation's core energy economy ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 25:22](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1522)). It depends on whether the leak opens new experiences or only adds tedium, and whether it sits in the core that everything else rests on. See [05. Systems and emergence](05-systems-and-emergence.md).

**Hand-made or generated, and should the seam show?** Ben Berman wants generated levels that look made by hand ([Ben Berman 2017, 12:39](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=759)), while Jon Perry stopped forcing Mini and Max's handcrafted areas to match its procedural ones because it made them worse ([Jon Perry 2025, 11:46](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=706)). Wildermyth weighs generated maps that multiplied cheaply against handcrafted maps that allowed pacing and unique goals but took long to make ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 21:42](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1302); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 23:21](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=1401)), and Sergio Garces finds hand-placing wins unless you invest heavily in the algorithm ([Sergio Garces 2022, 14:08](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=848)). It depends on where authored quality matters most, and whether the generated parts sit where looking generated is acceptable. See [09. Level generation](09-level-generation.md).

**Must every generated output be good?** Herbert Wolverson checks every result ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 24:35](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1475)), Sébastien Benard holds that a shipped generator must produce good output essentially every time ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 15:04](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=904)), and Brian Walker never lets a generator block progress ([Brian Walker 2018, 30:04](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1804)). Alexei Pepers reports that Caves of Qud keeps generators unconstrained until a specific harm is proven ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 40:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2437)), and Bjarke Alexander Larsen accepts unchecked randomness when players have a way to deal with bad outcomes ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 16:20](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=980)). It depends on who pays for a bad output: a player who cannot finish, or one who can route around it. See [11. Generative methods](11-generative-methods.md).

**Automate the effort, or keep it?** Josh Ge, Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup and Angband automate repetitive actions with one right answer ([Josh Ge 2016, 22:56](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1376); [bhauth 2020, 3:43](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=223); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 13:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=807)). Zeno Rogue leaves auto-travel out of HyperRogue because navigation is the challenge ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 18:02](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1082)), Martin Pichlmair values physical effort as part of the experience ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 30:10](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1810)), and Yong Zhen Zhou weighs the accessibility gained by simplifying physical inputs against the energy and fantasy it can strip away ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 16:23](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=983)), and Vagante makes menu time a risk ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 23:46](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1426)). For blind players, auto-explore is what makes exploration accessible, yet it leaves them disoriented, so Alexei Pepers would offer it as an option with orientation aids ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=280); [Alexei Pepers 2016, 26:53](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1613)). It depends on whether the effort is the game you are making, and for whom. See [13. Interface and accessibility](13-interface-and-accessibility.md).

**A shaped story, or an open one?** Tarn Adams found Dwarf Fortress's adventure mode flat without overarching structure and looks to villains' schemes for plot ([Tarn Adams 2018, 1:25](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=85); [Tarn Adams 2018, 5:59](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=359)), and Matt Carney gives every run a "pulse" such as descending a dungeon ([Matt Carney 2026, 22:58](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1378)). Emilia Lazer-Walker gave up on a shaped arc as too hard ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:19](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=979)), Cole Wehrle's Oath has no narrative framing ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 31:13](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1873)), and Tim Keenan left Duskers without a final resolution, though its players wanted one ([Tim Keenan 2017, 12:14](https://youtu.be/G5rq5ei2Lec?t=734)). Stephen G. Ware adds that emergent agent stories can only hope to hit required beats, while planners can guarantee them ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 3:07](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=187)). It depends on whether your game has beats that must land, and how much you will intervene behind the player's back. See [12. Narrative and worldbuilding](12-narrative-and-worldbuilding.md).

## A design brief for a new roguelike

Answer these in order when starting a new game. Each answer should fit in a sentence or two; if one does not, that is the part of the design to prototype first.

**The promise**

1. What should a run feel like, in one sentence, and is the game mainly about mastering a challenge, inhabiting a world, or a deliberate mix? See [01](01-what-is-a-roguelike.md).
